decision.reason: The current study (N = 263 twins aged 6–15; 107 DLD vs. 156 TD) explicitly introduces Bishop et al. (2014; PeerJ 2:e507, DOI 10.7717/peerj.507, and 2017 correction), which tested 11 four-year-olds with current language impairment versus 46 language-typical four-year-olds on the same animation-description fTCD paradigm (finding no significant within-group left-hemisphere bias in the n = 11 current-impairment subgroup, categorical group comparison p = .045, continuous LI p = .106; distinct from its broader N = 21 historical-concern sample and 51 Groen 2012 comparison cases). The current paper empirically retests whether children with DLD versus TD exhibit reduced left-hemisphere language lateralisation on the animation-description fTCD task using both continuous LI (p = .190) and categorical left/bilateral/right classifications. Under the codebook, retesting this empirical association in an older twin sample constitutes a conceptual replication despite age differences, within-group versus between-group analytical framing, or omission from the Discussion's parenthetical example citations (Illingworth & Bishop, 2009; Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008). It is distinct from shipped row 2411 (Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008) and all sibling targets.

decision.reason: Primary verification of both originals shows that Buss (2011; 10.1037/a0023227, target 0, which replaces shipped row 418 Phelps et al., 2016) and Buss et al. (2013; 10.1080/15374416.2013.769170) analyze the same N = 111 toddler cohort and age-2 fear predictor across different longitudinal follow-up waves. Buss (2011) already tested and reported longitudinal prediction from age-2 dysregulated fear to parent- and teacher-rated social inhibition/withdrawal across preschool (ages 24, 36, and 48 months on ITSEA/CBCL) and fall kindergarten (HBQ). Buss et al. (2013) added kindergarten laboratory stranger/peer free-play wariness observations, spring teacher-rated prosociality moderation, and age-6 clinical interview (ADIS) social anxiety disorder symptoms. The current study (N = 124 followed at 24, 36, and 48 months) measures only parent-reported preschool social inhibition (ITSEA at 24/36 months; HBQ at 48 months) and explicitly notes in Limitations that children were only followed to 48 months rather than kindergarten or clinical endpoints. Thus, the empirical test in the current study retests the Buss (2011) preschool parent-rated social inhibition finding (already captured under corrected row 418), not the distinct kindergarten laboratory/peer wariness, prosociality moderation, or age-6 ADIS clinical symptom findings of Buss et al. (2013).

Although the 2014 full text remains paywall-blocked and its institutional abstract summarizes only the four default systems and choice verification/adjustment without independently detailing the temporary contrast, the current paper explicitly attributes to van Dalen & Henkens (2014) the empirical finding that organ donation rates are higher when consent is temporary and renewable, predicts higher participation under temporary consent, empirically manipulates 3-year renewable versus permanent authorization in Sample 1 (N = 954), and tests the difference (chi-square = 1.94, p = .163). Under the codebook, this explicit empirical retest qualifies as a conceptual replication target despite the extension label and changed operationalization, and it is absent from shipped row 2383 (Johnson, Bellman, & Lohse, 2002) and sibling target 0 (Johnson & Goldstein, 2003).

Follow-up 0084 recovered the older 2013 five-method working paper (Jena 2013-009, N = 444), which compares five tasks between-subjects but also includes Section 6.5 / Table 8 analyzing within-person correlations (and Spearman robustness) between each subject's single assigned task and SOEP/DOSPERT questionnaires. decision.reason: Unlike the incomplete prior exclusion rationale assuming Csermely & Rabas (2016; 10.1007/s11166-016-9247-6) only examined temporal retest consistency and predictive validity, the complete primary XML recovered in follow-up 0082 (N = 96, Vienna laboratory) proves that Csermely & Rabas administered nine incentivised MPL lottery variants and two Dohmen willingness-to-risk survey items within-subjects and—separately from their 30-minute repeat (Sec 3.4/Table 9) and investment/auction prediction benchmarks (Sec 3.3/Tables 7–8)—directly tested simultaneous cross-method distributional differences (Sec 3.1/Table 4) and simultaneous within-person pairwise inter-method rank and ordinary correlations across tasks and questionnaires (Sec 3.2/Table 5; Appendix Table 10), finding generally weak inter-method rank agreement (only 11% significant at p < .001, alongside specific moderate positive correlations such as .33***, .44***, .39***, and survey .46***). The current study (N = 321) explicitly states that in line with Csermely & Rabas (2016) it explored the consistency of its three risk elicitation methods (REM1 hypothetical investment, REM2 Waerneryd questionnaire, REM3 paired lotteries) within-subjects, reporting pairwise correlations in Table 2 (.46***, .03, .19***). Under the codebook, this is a conceptual replication of Csermely & Rabas's simultaneous inter-method consistency finding, absent from shipped row 2431 (Carr & Steele, 2010) and all siblings.

Although the General Discussion explicitly states that their procedure is a close replication of the equivalent studies by Critcher & Gilovich (2008), Dogerlioglu-Demir & Koçaş (2015), and Koçaş & Dogerlioglu-Demir (2020), Studies 1–3 test direct positive high versus low restaurant anchors (Studio 97 vs. Studio 17), the Meta-Analysis and Note 2 pool only Critcher & Gilovich (2008) and Dogerlioglu-Demir & Koçaş (2015), and Note 1 states that Koçaş & Dogerlioglu-Demir (2020) explored how ambiguous anchor values (e.g., negative values) are interpreted. Because the 2020 primary full text is inaccessible in follow-up 0097 and its repository abstract describes shifting-decimal, negative, and inverse number associations without confirming whether a direct positive 17/97 WTP contrast was also tested, correspondence cannot be determined.
